utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Prosecution calls its next witness, Mina Zunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Yes, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Zunac. Could you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: My name is Mina Zunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Ms. Zunac, can you understand me clearly in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: Completely so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If at any time you're unable to understand me or if you don't understand one of my questions, please let me know, okay?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: Yes, of course,.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Ms. Zunac, I'm just going to go through a little bit of your background and if you can just confirm that it's accurate. You were born on the 5th of November 1974 and you are of Croatian ethnicity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You've lived in Zagreb all your life?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In 1992, did you start working?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was -- what did you start working at? What was the job that you started to do?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: The official title of my job is a customs broker or a certified custom representative as they call it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you still working in that position today?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In May of 1995, were you working in that position?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to turn now to the 2nd of May 1995. Were you working on that day?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In the morning of that day, the 2nd of May, can you tell us what you did and where you went?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: It was a routine working day. We had something to do at the customs office, then I was supposed to go to the bank and then to the national audit office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Before I ask you any more questions about this, could you tell me, if you remember, what kind of a day was it in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: Just like any other. The weather was fine. It was spring, sunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said it was a routine working day. Was it a working day for everybody or was it a holiday?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: For everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There was a -- it's a little unclear in the translation, what was it for everybody, a working day or a holiday?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: A working day for everybody, a regular day in mid-week.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were there people out in the street?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. It is the centre of town and also the business area. Therefore, there were a lot of people moving about, going about their business.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Before that date, the 2nd of May, 1995, to your knowledge, had there been any warning that Zagreb could be attacked?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: No. There were no indications that anything could take place. Furthermore, it was actually after all the air raids had finished and we enjoyed a relatively quiet period.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When had there been air raids, how long before, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: I can't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The alarm was sounded not the actual raids were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember if it had been that year or previous years or -- that the alarm was sounded?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: I can't be specific. It was a while ago, and the very events immediately before that and after I was wounded left some gaps in my memory. It is difficult for me to say exactly what had happened before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. In any event, on that day, on the 2nd of May, 1995, as you went about your business, did you have any reason to expect that there could be an attack on Zagreb that day?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you said in your previous answer that -- when I asked you what you were doing that day you said you were supposed to go to the national audit office. Did you get to the national audit office?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And can you tell me where that is located in terms -- you have some water there. Don't hesitate to -- if you need to drink some water. Can you tell me where that -- where the national audit office is located, in terms of what street and even if you know the address?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: The address is Schollosserove Stube number 1. It is in the centre of town at the crossroads Krizaniceva and Vlaska street. It is some five minutes away from Ban Jelisic square.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now what did you find when you got to the national audit office?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: It was a busy day in the centre. We took our car. That is my mother and I. We parked at Vlaska street and I went to the audit office to have some papers stamped. Then there was quite a queue at the audit offers and I went back to my mother to tell her that she should move on with her vehicle because she wasn't park in a marked spot and I told her that she can go on and that I would return home by foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Before we go on with your story, I'm going to make you look at some maps. If we could look at the map that is ERN 06010266 on e-court. This is a nicer version of a map which is in evidence as Exhibit 382. It's such a nice map, it takes a few seconds to load on e-court. If we could leave it just like that for the moment, Ms. Zunac, can you tell me just -- what this is in front of you, if you can see it? What is it a map of?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: I can see the map. It is the map of the centre of town, of the town of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'd like to do is admit into evidence one clean, unmarked verse of the map and then I'm going to ask the witness to mark it and that will be a separate exhibit. But I think it would be nice to have in evidence an unmarked version so if this could be admitted into evidence and given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The map on the screen is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that will be Exhibit number 814.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now if we could zoom in on the map and I'm interested in the part that is the -- it's really the upper right but not all the way upper right. Where it says Salata, before that if you take the arrow below, further down, further down, now to the right, there. That's -- I'd like to zoom in on that area, please. Yeah, a little bit more to the left. Sorry. Perfect. Thank you. Do you -- Ms. Zunac, are you able to recognise this area on the map, what is depicted there?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We can see here Stara Vlaska and Vlaska street as well as Draskoviceva street and the centre of town as well as the location where I was hit, I was wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to take our special pen and make a few markings if you could. First, are you able to see where Ban Jelacic square is on this map?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you put an A next to that?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Are you able to see Ilica Street on here?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: Yes, we can see the beginning of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you draw a line where it begins and put a B? And if you could put the B as close to the line as you can, please?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: This is Ilica that's where it begins.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If the record could reflect that the witness has drawn a line on the road leading from Ban Jelacic square and drew a line across the line indicating where the Ilica begins. So does is it your testimony then just to be clear about it that the Ilica goes from the Ban Jelacic square off in the direction to the left of the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just hold on, Witness. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An objection. I believe the witness should say herself what she marked on the map and what the lines and the markings concern, and not the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've marked the Ilica with a line which starts from Ban Jelacic square and moves on to -- towards the west, and in this case to the left of the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, I hear what Mr. Milovancevic is saying. I'm not quite clear I understand what he's saying. My concern is that I think you have been testifying. The concept of Ilica, the name Ilica first came from you and not from the witness. And I understand that this is all background information. But, you know, when we started I thought we were zooming in just below Salata, more to the right. Now we've gone to the -- you asked her to show this square and from then on you have been leading her. Maybe if you could ask her questions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour, though I do think that with respect to the Ilica street I just simply asked her if she knew -- could point to where it was and that's how we got into it. That was the first question, but I will continue and I will focus on the area where I've asked to zoom in on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, are you able to see on here on the map where the national audit office was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it no more? Is that national audit office no more? Does it no longer exist?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I don't know. I have -- actually don't know. I'm just interested in May of 1995. I don't know if it exists, if it's still there. I actually don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But in May of 1995, you testified that you went to the national audit office on the 2nd of May. Can you see where it is on the map?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: Yes. I can see the audit building on the map, and it is there, even today, but the institution merely changed its name. It is no longer the ZAP as it used to be referred to in Croatian. It is now called, FINA, F-I-N-A, but basically the same office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you take the pen and circle it and put a C next to the circle that you make?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: This is the audit office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now finally you testified earlier that you left the national audit office and went to speak to your mother who was in a parked car. Are you able to see on the map where approximately your mother was parked and where you went to speak with her?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: Yes. I can see it here. And more or less I can determine where the car was parked. Do you want me to mark that spot?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, if you would. If you could mark the spot and put a little D next to the spot where the car was parked?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: This is the approximate location of the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If the record could just reflect that the witness has put an X saying this is the approximate location of the car and has put a D above it. Your Honour, could this marked exhibit be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The marked exhibit is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That will be Exhibit number 815.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could just leave it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I see on the map that Draskoviceva Street runs south from the point you've marked as C. Can you tell me, describe for me what that street was and any significance of that street?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: It is a very busy street in the centre. What is important about it is that many tram lines intersect there from various parts of town. It is quite a busy street and it is a part of the business area. Do you want me to mark it on the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I should have done it before, I'm sorry. Yes. If you could mark -- are you able to see -- you said the trams intersect. Do you know what point on that street they intersect?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: In principle, those tram lines intersect in this part. Could we please zoom out?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yeah. Could we zoom back out? I think -- I think that's fine. Now, we lost your prior markings but that's okay. They are in evidence. If you're able now on this version to mark where the trams intersect on that street, Draskoviceva Street?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: Trams come from the direction of Vlaska which continues on towards Draskoviceva Street, then there is another line coming from up above, from Riblek [phoen] and another one from Borongaj, and also from the bottom of the map up the Draskoviceva there are trams coming from the trains -- central station, and then some of them go on towards Ban Jelacic square. So all these lines intersect in this area and a lot of people change trams right here in this street.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you -- just so our record is clear, you've drawn some arrows and a circle, can you put an A next to the area where these various trams intersect?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: This area marked with the letter A represents a tram stop on both sides of the street where many tram lines meet and where people usually change tram lines and that's the central portion of the Draskoviceva.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Zunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour could this marked map now be admitted into evidence and given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This marked map is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit number 816.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you to look at another map and this is Exhibit 805, please, in evidence, and we need to look at page 7. If we could just zoom in on it a little bit, not too much but just make it a little bit bigger? Now, Ms. Zunac, do you recognise this map? Are you able to orient yourself on this map?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: I recognise this map and I can get my bearings on it easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On this map, could you mark -- are you able to see where the national audit office was on this map? Was and is.

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: It is clearly visible where the audit office is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you just mark it with an A?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is it visible on this map where your car was, where your mother was parked, where you went to speak with her?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: Yes. That can be seen here. I can determine an approximate location of the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you mark that with a B, please?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this marked map now be admitted into evidence and given a number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The marked map is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number 817.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay, we're done with maps. Ms. Zunac, I want to continue now with the story of what happened that day. When I interrupted you, you said that you had returned to the car and you were speaking to your mother at the car. What happened next?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: We exchanged but a few words and after that, first we heard an explosion and then everything fell silent. It seemed as if everything had stopped and as if we were in a vacuum. It lasted for a few seconds, but to us it appeared to be much longer. After that, we heard a series of small explosions. It all happened within a moment of time. After that I felt pain in my leg and I could see that my leg had been blown apart. At first, I wasn't clear as to what was happening. It was so unexpected and it was such a surprise. I was in a state of shock. After that, people began panicking, one could hear screams, and mayhem was created.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Ms. Zunac, when the explosion occurred, where were you precisely in relation to the car?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: I was next to the driver's seat, outside of the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And where was your mother?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: My mother was inside the car, sitting in the driver's seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And after people began panicking and mayhem was created, what's the next thing that happened?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: My mother was in a state of shock and panic. One could hear more explosions in the background, and I tried walking towards other cars that were parked there because I was in the open, but I couldn't stand on the leg, and I realised that it had been shattered to pieces. I threw myself on the ground and I crawled to find a place between the cars. Fuel was leaking from all the tanks, and all the cars around me were damaged. People were screaming around me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: Something was ablaze and somebody started yelling, "Fire," which I found terrible because I was lying in a pool of fuel that was leaking from the surrounding vehicles, and I saw a man running by the vehicles with an extinguisher. I grabbed him by his leg and I asked him to spray the area around me because I was afraid that I would be caught by the fire. When the man saw the condition I was in, he stopped my bleeding, he did it with his belt, and he sprayed the area around me with the fire extinguisher. After that, my mother got out of the car. He [as interpreted] was in a total shock, in a state of panic. And the people in the cars realised that something had happened to me. They got out of their cars, they came closer to me but they were not moving. They didn't know what to do with me. After a while, the man who had stopped my leg from bleeding returned with a young policeman and they tried to help me. They tried to call an ambulance but this was not possible because traffic was in a state of collapse and the telephone lines were down and although hospital was near, they could not get an ambulance. So they decided to transport me themselves, but they did not have a vehicle handy that they could use. All the cars in the vicinity were damaged and were not in driving condition. This young policeman went somewhere and he returned with a vehicle that he could use, but then they had another problem. They could not carry me to that vehicle and they could not bring that vehicle towards me because there were a lot of debris and unexploded bomblets around me and they didn't dare enter the street with that vehicle. They tried to find a stretcher. They couldn't, and after a while, they took a door from a building, they put me on the door and they started carrying me slowly from that street towards that car that they had been able to locate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that something was ablaze. Were you able to determine what it was that was ablaze?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: No. At that moment, I was focused on myself and my wounds, and I did not pay too much attention to what was burning around me. I only heard people repeating, "fire, fire."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that the man stopped the bleeding in your leg with his belt. Can you tell us exactly how he did that, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: First he removed his belt, and then he ligated my wound on my hip. He tried to tie as a knot as tightly as possible without aggravating my wound even further.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us in what direction you were carried on this door that they used for a stretcher?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: They carried me in the direction of west, towards the Ban Jelacic square. They went in that direction because I assume that the situation was even worse towards Draskoviceva. I suppose they didn't even attempt to go along Draskoviceva but rather decided to carry me westward and that's where the vehicle was that they had managed to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: After that, they took me to the trauma centre, to the hospital that is in Draskoviceva, south of the intersection of Draskoviceva and Vlaska, approximately five to ten minutes' walk from the place where I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After you were injured and while you were being carried on that door, did you -- do you recall seeing any other injured people?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you whether I saw any wounded. I saw a man lying next to a car parked in Vlaska. There were no people around him, nobody came to his assistance, and I suppose that he was already dead and that's why they focused their attention on me rather than him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Before the explosion occurred, did you see any military personnel or any military vehicles in the area where you were?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: No. This is the centre of town. There were no uniformed men there. There were no military there. There are no military facilities there. The only uniformed person that I could see there was this young policeman, but he was not a military policeman, he was a police officer, maybe a traffic police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you describe for us now the injuries that you received as a result of the explosion?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: I suffered serious injuries in my right leg. My right foot was shattered. One part of my foot was amputated. My lower right leg was heavily damaged. I had a fracture of my right knee, right hip, my right fist, and I also sustained head injuries. I had a head full of shrapnels. My whole back was black and blue with contusions. I was fortunate enough to have been wearing a leather motorcycle jacket, so quite a number of shrapnels could not penetrate that thick jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to start with the injury on your right fist and then we'll talk about your leg and your foot. Is there any -- today is there any visible sign of the injury to your hand? Your right-hand?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: Yes. There are scars. You can see a plate let in my right fist. I am missing a bone so this has been replaced. I cannot close my fist and I have a lot of problems when I write because I cannot hold a pen for any length of time, and I can't write for any length of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you think you could hold up your right hand for us and we will be able to see it on the monitor. If you could just sort of show where the -- and if you could just point to us where the injury is, where the scar is and the injury on your hand?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: [Indicates] This is my right fist and this part is a metal plate. These are scars on this part, and on the upper part of my fist, the mobility of my fingers has been reduced. I cannot close my fist properly. Also, after that injury, I stopped playing the piano.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll ask you more about that in a moment. I want to ask you about the injury to your leg and foot, and to spare you from having to remove your shoe in court, we've taken some photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if we could show them on the E court it's ERN 06010262 to 0265. We are looking at the photograph which -- the first photograph in the series which has the number 0262.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Ms. Zunac, do you recognise that, what's depicted in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: Yes. This is my right leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we turn to the -- could we look at the next page, please? This is 0263. Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: Yes. My right foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at the next picture 0264? What is that, in 0264?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: You can see the big scar that I have on the right knee.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Finally if we could look at 0265, please? What is that?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: This is the sole of my right leg, and you can again see a big scar there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: By the way, can you tell us what kind of a shoe were you wearing on that day?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: This is very important for the way I was injured. I was wearing a motorcycle boots with protector parts, very thick leather with a very thick sole, and I believe that those boots were the one that is saved my leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could these photographs be admitted into evidence and given a number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The photographs are admitted into evidence. May they please be given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That will be Exhibit 818.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Ms. Zunac, and they can be taken off the screen now. Ms. Zunac, did the doctors remove the shrapnel from your foot and leg?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: No. For the most part, no. I have over 45 shrapnels still in my leg, which are impossible to remove. One could remove one by one, if there is pain or further impairments but it is in practical terms impossible to remove all those shrapnels from my leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long did you spend in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: All in all, about a year. It is important to stress here that I would be discharged from time to time because the hospitals were crowded and they needed beds, so between surgeries I would be discharged and also I live some ten minutes from the hospital and in case of any complications that might have occurred, I could have been transported back to the hospital in no time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You made a reference to surgeries in that last answer. How many surgeries did you have?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: I had seven surgeries during the first couple of months, and after that three more, and then I stopped counting after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Ms. Zunac, I want to show you some photographs. There are Exhibit 386 and if we could start with page 4 of that exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if we could zoom in a little bit on photograph F1, the one on the top, Ms. Zunac, do you recognise that, what's depicted in photograph F1?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: F1 depicts Draskoviceva street.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look now, please, at page 18 of this exhibit? And I'm looking for photograph F30, if we could zoom in on that. Can you tell us what's depicted in this photograph, F30?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: This is the crossroads of Draskoviceva and Vlaska and in the background you see the building of the audit office where I was headed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go to page 28, please? I want to look at photograph F50. And could we zoom in more on this? Maybe even more, if we could, just one more. On those cars in the middle there. That's perfect. Ms. Zunac, do you recognise anything in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: This is Vlaska street, where I got injured, and you can see my vehicle, if you look at the middle line, the third vehicle from the front, the green Renault, the first car is white, and then the green one, that's my car.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we ask with the assistance of the usher maybe you can mark it with a pen. I think your description was clear but just so we are sure. If you could just draw an arrow pointing to your car in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: Here it is. This is my car.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this marked photograph now be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The marked photograph is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit number 819, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we now go to page 30? And I want to look at photograph F52. Actually, if I could just have a moment, that wasn't the one I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: You can see my vehicle in this photo as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Well, can you describe for us where it is in this photograph? This is F52.

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: The vehicle is left to the cars parked on the right-hand side of the road. In other words, it is the third car in the middle of the photo, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not inclined to have the witness mark it unless Your Honours would prefer. Okay, thank you. The photograph I had in mind was the next photograph, it's F53 on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise anything in this photograph, F53?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: Yes. Again, this is Vlaska street taken from a different angle, and you can see the car and the man lying on the street that we passed as they were carrying me. He's dead, and you can see that he's lying next to his car.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And finally, could we go to page 36 and look at photograph F65? Do you recognise anything in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: Vlaska street and in the left bottom corner you can see my vehicle, and this is the place where I was injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions about those photographs. So they can be taken off the monitor. Ms. Zunac, I want to talk to you about the present day, about today. Do you have any physical or psychological effects from your injuries today? Maybe start with the physical.

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: I do. I have constant pain in my leg. I have problems walking. I limp. From time to time, I feel strong pain in the toe that was amputated, and this pain is the worst because I feel pain in the part of my body that no longer exists. I can feel changes when the weather changes. I also have problems with my right hand, problems with writing, as I've already told you. I can no longer play the piano. My leg injuries have changed my way of life. I can no longer ski. I can no longer engage in a majority of physical activities that I used to enjoy. At first I could not move properly. Now this has improved but this has had an impact on my social life. I could not go out. I could not keep pace with my friends. I could no longer engage in the things that we used to do together in the past. This was no longer possible. I still have a lot of problems with choosing my foot wear because in addition to my right foot being painful, I cannot move my right ankle and therefore, I cannot wear most of the shoes that are available, and that is what creates a lot of problems in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Ms. Zunac, have there been any psychological effects?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: Of course. At first, after I was injured, I had problems with open spaces. I did not dare go out too much, and when I did, I would always stick to the buildings. I fretted open spaces, although I knew in my mind that nothing else could happen, I still felt the discomfort in open spaces. I had a lot of problems with short-term memory, with events that took place in the not-distant past. Sometimes I have problems with chronologically putting things in order. I have a lot of problems sleeping. I suffer from insomnia. Any sudden, unexpected noises cause discomfort and fear. Initially, if, for example, the doors slammed or the windows slammed, this sudden noise would make me throw myself on the floor, which was so silly. Later on it stopped but at first I really felt uncomfortable with that. And also, another thing that is very traumatic is, for example, celebration of new year, when there are crackers being fired and that period of year re-enacts my trauma and, if I possibly can, I don't like being in town around new year.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Zunac. Those are all my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence has no questions for the witness, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: No questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Zunac, are you able to tell us what happened to your mother on that day?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: Fortunately, she wasn't injured, but she suffered a great shock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And was your mother's car or your car, was it also not damaged?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: The car had been almost completely destroyed, but I don't believe that to be important. It's but a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You told us that you still have shrapnel in your body that has not been removed. Does it have any effect on you, physically or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: The problem with the pieces of shrapnel is that there are too many, and the doctors do not dare try and remove them. More or less, I have to be alert all the time. I have to be watchful because should there be any pain or any significant change, I need to contact my physicians. The problem is that they cannot offer any sort of advice as regards those pieces of shrapnel. I can do everything but at the same time I can't do anything. I have to be on constant alert to watch for any sudden changes in my leg, and should that happen, I have to get in touch with them as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand. I guess what I want to find out is whether they hurt. Do you hurt as a result of this shrapnel, even today, or don't you feel anything? That's what I meant by what effect do they have on you.

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: The pain in my leg is a constant one, and I don't perceive it solely as something caused by shrapnel, because I can't locate the exact source. It is always there but one gets used to it. You feel it, but you are no longer hindered by it, although on occasion you are sharply reminded of it because it increases in intensity and then it starts obstructing your activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able -- can you tell us what you work -- you told us that you work as a customs broker or certified customs representative. What do you do in your work?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: I prepare documentation concerning the goods that need to be taxed by the customs. I usually work as an administrator. I prepare the documentation needed for import or export of goods in and out of the country, including the shipping, the forwarding, and I submit those papers to the customs office, as well as I follow the goods through from point A to point B, from the person selling to the person buying and the other way around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As a result of the injuries that you sustained, are you -- let me put it differently. Are you able to do your work now after your injuries as you were able to do it before the injuries?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: Not any longer, because it included a lot of work being done in the field, whereas now I work mainly in the office and I go to only one customs office. Before that, I could perform my duties in a better way, could move about physically much more. Unfortunately I can no longer do that any more. Therefore I spend most of the time in my office, and in the customs office that is nearby. To make this clearer perhaps, there are in total eight customs offices in Zagreb, five principal ones and three branch offices in various locations but I only go to that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I know you've told us that you are not able to write for any length of time. You've told us that you're not able to play the piano. Are you able to type on the computer?

utterances.speaker: MINA ZUNAC
utterances.text: In principle, yes, because what I need to do in the course of my work is fill out forms, and I have to do that in handwriting, so I have to do that more than typing on a computer itself. Therefore, the typing is not that much of a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Zunac. I don't have any further questions for you. Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, no further questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Zunac, thank you so much for coming. This brings us to the end of your testimony in court. On behalf of the Tribunal and the Chamber, I would like to say thank you to you for availing yourself to come and testify and let us know what happened to you. As I say we have come to the end of your testimony. You are excused from further attending court and you may stand down. Once again, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I suppose I don't have to say Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You do, Your Honour, I'm afraid. There are a few small housekeeping matters that we need to take care of before we rest our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The first is that at long last, we have a clean, nice version of the agreed facts that we need to admit into evidence as an exhibit as requested by the Trial Chamber. So if I could hand this up, and I have a copy for the Defence which, of course, they already have it but if I could just provide it to the court so that it could be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Has this been filed?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm filing it now, Your Honour, if it could be given a number now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay do you want this to be given to the Registry?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. I have extra copies for Your Honours if that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours that will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you do that I'm sorry, I beg your pardon, I've got to find out from Mr. Milovancevic if he confirms the agreed facts. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we've agreed with the OTP on the facts. Since I have been given this document at the same time you are, I believe it to be containing the facts that we have agreed on but therefore, yes, I can confirm that we agree with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. May -- I beg your pardon. The document headed agreed facts is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That will be Exhibit number 820.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just so there is no confusion I've been dealing with Mr. Sekulic on the Defence team on this, and we've been going back and forth and he confirmed this morning by e-mail that this was what the Defence would agree to, just not to leave the impression that I dropped this on the Defence this morning because it's actually been going back and forth for some weeks now. Just a few other small matters that needs to be dealt with. We of course the Prosecution decided to drop Witness Slobodan Lazarevic and at the time we did, we agreed that his testimony -- his written evidence and his exhibits would drop out of the case. We never formally said which exhibits those were. I think it would be good to clear that, make that clear on the record. Exhibits 429 through Exhibit 544 [sic] should drop out. They should be taken out, removed from the record. And I think that's something that the registrar can do outside of court but I think it's important that it be on the record that those exhibits no longer are part of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May Exhibits 429 through 544 please be dropped out of the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm sorry before that happens there is a -- was an error on the transcript or else I misspoke. It's actually 429 to 455.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay 429 to 455. Those exhibits must be dropped out and that can be done out of court?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The third matter, Your Honour, is that as I understand it, everything is being done with respect to Exhibits 24, 476 and 238. Those are the three books where each party -- each side made selections and I think those are still in the process of being -- the selections are being put into e-court and given assigned numbers. But I don't think there is -- I just wanted to note on the record that that process is still being done and it will be completed, I think, in the next few days. Secondly, the Trial Chamber at one point inquired about Exhibits 258 and 380, which it quite correctly observed were the same exhibit. I think what's been done with that is that the exhibit will be now known as 258 and exhibit 380 will be eliminated as a duplicate. So that will drop out and that evidence will be -- that exhibit will just be 258. There was also a problem with respect to Exhibits 396 and 397. The 92 bis statement of a witness, MM-044, had been divided up into two parts. The way that's been resolved is that it's being re-uploaded, the exhibit's been re-uploaded and will be exhibit 396 and so exhibit 397 will become free and will no longer be a number, no longer be an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, the Chamber is aware of that and I believe that Registry is also going on, both -- on both issues, that is exhibits 24 to 38 and 476. It's working on that and the Chamber is also is aware the Registry is presumed working on exhibits 258 to 380, 396 through to 397.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There is just one more. The 92 bis packages of witnesses MM-032 and MM-024 which the Court just admitted into evidence by its decision a few days ago, those are also being uploaded into e-court and will be assigned exhibit numbers by the registrar, but of course that will occur in the next few days. But that is being tended to as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if those are all the housekeeping matters, if I could just -- before I close I just want to make -- I just want to note one thing and that is that at the beginning of the case, the Prosecution predicted that its case would take 298 hours to try, which amounts to approximately 80 days. We've brought it in under 260 hours, 69 days of testimony. I just wanted to note that before we close. With that, the Prosecution rests its case against the accused Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. If I may take a moment to also raise a housekeeping matter, on the 14th of June 2006, the Prosecution filed a response to Milutinovic's motion for access to certain confidential filings in this case. And in its response the Prosecution also assented to the applicant's access to certain portions of the requested filings. What the Chamber would like to know is whether in the Prosecution's view, those portions that are being required include any information which requires consent by the provider of the information under Rule 70(B) because if that be the case, then the provider of that information must first consent before -- do we need private session for this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I was thinking about that. But I think so far, no, it's sufficiently vague so that I don't think that's necessary. The answer -- I appreciate the inquiry, Your Honour. The answer is no, consent is not required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No 70(B) consent is required?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're absolutely sure of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The next question would then be: Does the Prosecution consent to the could accused of Milutinovic also accessing those portions? Because they are going to be public information in that court to the extent that those co-accused may be called public.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, we would consent to that with the understanding and I think what Your Honour just said, that that is that it would be confidential in that court. That is, that it would just go to the co-accused but that it would remain confidential and would not become public in that proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Has the Prosecution made that a condition of their consent?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, all the filings have been confidential so I thought it was implicit in this process that it would be -- that it would remain confidential in that proceeding. But if it's not clear, yes, we would make that a condition that this be done confidentially, that the parties in that proceeding can have it, but that it not be made public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. If I remember well, Mr. Milovancevic, the Defence had indicated that the Defence is not opposed to availing this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. In that event, then the decision will be made accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry I just remembered that there was one other housekeeping matter that was left over from yesterday. And that is the evidence of MM-080. Your Honours had proposed unredacting certain portions. The Prosecution has agreed and as I understood from the transcript yesterday, the Defence wanted to check it one more time before they took a position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Milovancevic yesterday you asked for time to check whether what your position would be with regard to witness MM-080; correctly put, MM-080's testimony that needs to be unredacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we sought no protective measures and we agree with the position of the Chamber that the measures in this case be removed or to be more specific to have this text made public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. An oral order will then be plead with respect to that evidence of MM-080 in due course. Any other outstanding matters, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm wondering if anybody knows when we are sitting next Monday? I don't think we appear on the calendar, just out of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Next Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Whether we are in the morning or afternoon, for the 98 bis submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Next Monday is the 26th. According to my diary we are supposed to be sitting in this Court at quarter past 2.00. Let me just double-check. Well, the schedule that is dated the 12th of June doesn't have us sitting on that day, which is surprising.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Registry has just kindly offered that they will check this and let us know, because according to this latest schedule, we are not supposed to be sitting on that day but earlier we were supposed to be sitting, as I said, at quarter past 2.00. So we will probably adjourn to Monday, the 26th, without a court and time. We'll hear, okay? Is that okay? In that event, then the Court adjourns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 26th day of June, 2006.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.25 a.m.,
